newsitem.title: USA: TENNIS-U.S. GRABS 2-0 LEAD OVER SPAIN IN FED CUP FINAL.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-U.S. GRABS 2-0 LEAD OVER SPAIN IN FED CUP FINAL.

text.p: Monica Seles and Lindsay Davenport put the United States in the driver's seat in the Fed Cup finals on Saturday, giving the home team a comfortable 2-0 lead over defending champions Spain with overpowering victories.

Co-world number one Seles played a near perfect first set and fought through some nervous moments in the second to complete a 6-2 6-4 victory over Conchita Martinez that put the pressure squarely on the Spaniards.
"It felt much easier going in there 1-0 up," Davenport said of her Olympic final rematch with Arantxa Sanchez Vicario in the day's second match. "I think that did make a huge difference."
Spain's number one appeared to respond well to the pressure by jumping out to a 5-3 lead over a slow-starting Davenport.
But the Atlanta gold medallist lifted her game to Olympian heights to stun Sanchez 7-5 6-1.
The towering Davenport won 10 of the last 11 games from the speedy Spaniard in front of an embarrassingly small but appreciative crowd at the Atlantic City Convention Centre.
"I couldn't ask for anything more," said U.S. captain Billie Jean King of her squad's 2-0 lead.
The United States, which lost the last two Fed Cup finals to Spain, will now have three chances to clinch the title Sunday, beginning with Seles, who takes on Sanchez in the first reverse singles.
Seles, who raised her record to 10-0 against Martinez, takes a 12-1 mark versus Sanchez into Sunday's match.
"They have a difficult task but not impossible," King said of Spain's dwindling chances at a fourth consecutive title. "I wouldn't want to go to bed down 0-2."
Seles, playing for the first time in a final for a team rather than just for herself, was in the proverbial zone in the first set against Martinez, who looked to be sleep walking early.
Seles used deep, powerful groundstrokes to keep Martinez off balance and was perfection from the service line.
The Yugoslav-turned-American served four love games and broke Martinez in the fourth and eighth games to take the set.
The Spaniard woke up in the second set, breaking a suddenly nervous Seles in the opening game.
"In the second set when I lost that game I was more nervous than I should have been," Seles admitted.

"In the first set I was just zoning in everything and it's very hard to continue that. Everyone was saying perfect tennis, great tennis, but where can you go from here, I can only go down and that's what happened."
When Seles missed her third chance to break back in the key sixth game, she confirmed her status as an all-American tennis star by getting cited for an audible obscenity.
John McEnroe and Andre Agassi would have been proud.
"That's never happened before," said Seles, blushing and giggling. "I have never been so rattled as I was today."
But even a rattled Seles is a force to be reckoned with, and two points later she had her service break, bringing the first roar from the sparse crowd.
Martinez put up more of a fight the rest of the way, but Seles wanted no part of a third set and she broke the Spaniard for the match in the 10th game to take the heat off Davenport.
Davenport also admitted to a bad case of nerves early, and crafty veteran Sanchez looked on her way to leveling the tie when she served for the first set at 5-4.
But the American started belting winners with carefree abandon and Sanchez suddenly had no answer for Davenport's punishing strokes.
Davenport won 23 of her last 24 service points, ending the match with consecutive aces.
"I let her back into the match when she was not feeling so well, so comfortable on the court," Sanchez said.
"I was playing really well and suddenly I felt like it went away."
A beaming Davenport, who was swarmed by her teammates after the win, was obviously proud that she has added a tougher mental attitude to her game.

"At 5-3 I was able to hold and then finally get a few balls in and break her and then from there I just felt so much more comfortable, so much more relaxed and really confident to go for my shots," she said of the turning point.
"So many times in the past I've gotten down and kind of stayed down, not fought back.
"Today I was able to turn it around."
